content: Mechanical or infectious complications frequently necessitate the removal or replacement of peripheral intravenous (PIV) catheters in neonates. Heparin has demonstrated efficacy in prolonging the patency of peripheral arterial and central venous catheters. However, its use carries the risk of life-threatening complications, particularly in preterm neonates. The primary aim of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness of heparin, compared to placebo or no treatment, in extending the duration of PIV catheter patency in neonates requiring such catheters. A comprehensive literature search was conducted across multiple databases, including MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, covering publications from their inception up to February 2005. Abstracts from major pediatric research societies were also reviewed. No language restrictions were applied, and the search was updated in 2010. The inclusion criteria for the review were randomized or quasi-randomized trials comparing heparin, administered either as a flush or infusion, to placebo or no treatment. Studies were required to involve a neonatal population and report at least one relevant outcome. Data collection and analysis were performed following the guidelines of the Cochrane Neonatal Review Group. Ten studies met the eligibility criteria. Heparin was administered either as a flush solution or as an additive to total parenteral nutrition. Five studies provided data on the duration of the first catheter's use. Among these, two studies found no statistically significant effect of heparin, two studies reported a statistically significant increase in catheter duration, and one study observed a statistically significant decrease in catheter duration in the heparin group. The studies exhibited significant variability in methodological quality, heparin dosage, timing, route of administration, and reported outcomes. Due to these differences, the results were not pooled for meta-analysis. Additionally, individual studies did not report significant differences between the heparin and placebo/no treatment groups in terms of risks for complications such as infiltration, phlebitis, or intracranial hemorrhage. The authors concluded that there is insufficient evidence to determine the effectiveness of heparin in prolonging PIV catheter use in neonates. As a result, no recommendations can be made regarding the routine use of heparin in this population. Further research is necessary to establish the efficacy, optimal dosing, and safety profile of heparin in neonates with PIV catheters.
